text: The Taliban released a biography of reclusive founder Mullah Mohammed Omar to quell rumors of his death and assert his leadership. The 11-page document, published on the group's website, details his life and current role to counter the rise of ISIS.
Hundreds attended Walter Scott's funeral, where his death was mourned as a catalyst for change. The officer who shot Scott was charged with murder, though conflicting witness accounts have emerged.

Former TSA agent Daniel Boykin was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly filming a co-worker and burglarizing her home. He pleaded guilty to charges including unlawful photography and aggravated burglary.

Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to boost its economy, lacking traditional natural resources. The country hosts events like the Kriol Jazz Festival and Atlantic Music Expo to attract international tourism and exposure.
Arsenal beat Burnley 1-0 to keep their title hopes alive, moving within four points of leaders Chelsea. The victory was secured by a first-half goal from Aaron Ramsey.

Twin Peaks' original cast backs David Lynch in his salary dispute with Showtime, releasing a video supporting the #SaveTwinPeaks campaign. The actors argue the revival cannot proceed without its creator, who exited over insufficient funds to complete the scripts.
Andrew Getty, 47, an heir to the Getty oil fortune, was found dead at his Los Angeles home. Authorities report the death appears to be from natural causes, with no foul play suspected.

A Maryland woman, Nyia Parler, is in custody after allegedly leaving her quadriplegic son in a Philadelphia park for days to visit her boyfriend. She cannot be extradited to face charges until completing an unspecified treatment.
NASA scientist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai. The asteroid, discovered in 2010, was named to honor the activist's contributions and to inspire young women.
Gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 people aboard the Celebrity Infinity cruise ship. The CDC is investigating the cause, which has affected both passengers and crew.
"Star Wars" saga released on digital HD. Mindy Kaling's brother admitted to faking his race for medical school. Burger King sponsored a wedding for a couple with the same last name.
FBI charges Philadelphia woman Keonna Thomas with attempting to join ISIS after she purchased a ticket to Turkey. Two New York women were also arrested on separate terror charges.

HBO released a teaser for the second season of "True Detective," premiering June 21. The new season stars Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch in a story of murder and conspiracy in California.

Carlos Colina, 32, was charged with assault and improper disposal of a body after human remains were found in a duffel bag and an apartment building in Cambridge. The victim was identified as Jonathan Camilien, 26, and police are investigating if additional charges are warranted.

Louisville basketball star Trey Moses asked high school freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to be his prom date. The gesture, which included flowers and a Taylor Swift-themed poster, has gone viral and highlights the school's Best Buddies program.

NBC debuts "A.D. The Bible Continues," a 12-week sequel to the hit miniseries, airing just in time for Easter. The show chronicles the aftermath of Jesus' resurrection and the early days of Christianity.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence signed a controversial religious freedom law to bolster conservative credentials for a potential 2016 presidential run. The move has ignited a national backlash but also solidified support among the GOP's ultraconservative base, pulling the entire Republican field further to the right.

Apple released a new mobile OS update with more diverse emojis, including various skin tones, same-sex couples, and new flags. The update has sparked varied reactions, with some praising the inclusivity and others criticizing omissions like redheads.

Singer Avril Lavigne reveals she was bedridden for five months with Lyme disease, explaining her mysterious absence from the public eye. The Canadian singer, now "80 percent better," says the illness was a "wake-up call" and is releasing new music.

New research indicates Anne Frank and her sister died at least a month earlier than previously thought, likely in February 1945 from typhus at Bergen-Belsen. The Anne Frank House study, based on survivor testimonies and archives, contradicts the official date of death and shows the sisters were closer to surviving the Holocaust.

Two Troy University students were arrested in Florida for allegedly gang raping a woman during spring break. The suspects were identified after police found video of the assault during an unrelated investigation.

A Washington state dog survived being hit by a car, bludgeoned with a hammer, and buried alive, staggering to a farm four days later. The one-year-old bully mix, named Theia, is now receiving extensive medical care after a fundraising campaign surpassed its $10,000 goal.

FBI confirms Malaysian bomb maker Marwan was killed in a January raid in the Philippines. The operation, which resulted in the deaths of 44 elite police commandos, was marred by controversy and threatened a regional peace agreement.

Critics argue the Iran nuclear deal surrenders crucial leverage, rewarding the terrorist-supporting state with sanctions relief while allowing it to maintain its nuclear infrastructure. The agreement, they warn, lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent cheating, drawing parallels to past failed deals like the one with North Korea.
"Mad Men" concludes its run, reflecting the tumultuous end of the 1960s. The finale is expected to address major events of the era while resolving the fates of its central characters.
Dallas Zoo giraffe Katie gave birth to a 6-foot-tall calf in a live, hour-long broadcast. The newborn is reportedly healthy, nursing and standing, joining its 4-year-old sister.

President Obama's historic nominee for attorney general, Loretta Lynch, faces a record-breaking delay for a confirmation vote, sparking accusations of racial bias from supporters. Senate Republicans deny the delay is racially motivated, attributing it instead to partisan battles over unrelated legislation.
Three people were killed and five wounded in an attack on the attorney general's office in Balkh province. Security forces are engaged in an ongoing firefight with the assailants.
TV legend Bob Barker, 91, returned to host "The Price Is Right" for the first time since 2007. Barker handled the first game before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey.

Blues legend B.B. King, 89, was hospitalized for dehydration related to his Type II diabetes but has since been released and is recovering at home. The "King of the Blues" thanked fans for their concern and is now resting with his family.

Jurors found Dzhokhar Tsarnaev guilty on all counts in the Boston Marathon bombing. To prevent future extremism, the author argues that young Muslims must be shown that violence harms, rather than helps, their community.

CNN highlights top videos of the week, including a tour of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion, the world's tallest roller coaster, and a tearful interview with a former student of Bikram Choudhury. Other segments feature a witness to the Germanwings crash, a panel on Indiana's religious freedom law, and a study on celebrity facial attractiveness.

Pentagon map shows coalition forces have retaken 25-30% of ISIS-held Iraqi territory. Analysts warn ISIS is adapting, using asymmetric attacks to offset losses and maintain its image of success. The coalition's conventional strategy is criticized for not employing more advanced maneuverist warfare.

Air Canada passenger Oliver Minatel was choked by a fellow traveler on a flight from Toronto to Atlanta. The suspect was subdued by other passengers and taken into custody by authorities upon landing.
British banker Rurik Jutting was charged with murdering two women in his Hong Kong apartment. A court hearing to determine if there is enough evidence for a trial was adjourned until May.

A deadly tornado tore through Illinois, killing one person in Fairdale and causing widespread damage in Rochelle. The storm flattened homes, trapped residents, and forced responders to navigate debris-choked roads as severe weather continued to plague the Midwest.

Don McLean's handwritten lyrics for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction. The famed manuscript, which includes unused lines and notes, fetched the third-highest price ever for an American literary manuscript.
UNRWA chief to visit Yarmouk camp to assess humanitarian crisis. The visit aims to address the suffering of 18,000 civilians trapped in the besieged camp.

Saudi-led coalition airstrikes and ground fighting in Yemen have killed over 600 people and destroyed infrastructure, leaving millions without power. The International Committee of the Red Cross is struggling to deliver aid as the conflict escalates.

Legendary Australian cricketer and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died at 84 after a battle with skin cancer. Revered as one of cricket's greatest figures, Benaud was a record-breaking player and the sport's most iconic commentator.
A rare, nearly five-minute total lunar eclipse, the shortest of the century, occurred this morning. The event was best viewed in western North America and parts of Asia and South America.

Federal grand jury charges millionaire Robert Durst with unlawful firearm possession. The indictment is the latest legal hurdle for Durst, who also faces a first-degree murder charge in Los Angeles and awaits extradition.

"Furious 7" is released, offering fans a chance to remember the late Paul Walker, who died during filming. The film uses special effects and body doubles to complete his scenes and features a touching tribute to the actor.

"TheThe Price Is Right" model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed the winning price for a new car during a game, prompting host Drew Carey to jokingly award it to the contestant. The incident occurred on the heels of former host Bob Barker's surprise appearance on the show.

Thai Smile unveiled a new Airbus A320 featuring "Adventure Time" characters Jake, Finn, and Princess Bubblegum. The themed plane, part of a partnership with Cartoon Network, will make its inaugural flight from Bangkok to Phuket on April 4.
Pedestrians in Washington, D.C., halted traffic to help a mother duck and her brood of ducklings safely cross a busy street. The group, including a CNN crew, guided the family to a safer grassy area.

French police have completed evidence collection at the Germanwings crash site, leaving a private security firm to guard the location. Investigators have recovered the plane's black boxes and identified 150 DNA profiles from the remains of the 150 victims.

Cuba and the U.S. attend the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962, as Washington is expected to remove Cuba from its list of state sponsors of terrorism. The historic thaw in relations is complicated by Cuba's close ties to Venezuela and a public brawl between government supporters and dissidents in Panama.

Jesus' ministry was funded by donations from wealthy supporters, including women like Mary Magdalene and Joanna, who provided for the group from their own resources. The movement operated at a subsistence level, relying on this financial backing to sustain its itinerant mission.

California regulators have ordered PG&E to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe pipeline operations, including the deadly 2010 San Bruno explosion. The bulk of the fine will fund mandated pipeline safety improvements.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old who inspired millions with her fight against brain cancer and her collegiate basketball game, has died. Her story raised $1.4 million for cancer research and was celebrated as a legacy of courage and perseverance.

A major fire erupted at a Louisville, Kentucky, industrial park Friday morning, sending thick smoke and flames into the air. Authorities reported no injuries as they worked to contain the blaze at the General Electric facility.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, a key figure in nuclear talks, has a complex history including U.S. education, a past role in the Iranian Revolution, and discrepancies in his official biography. He has engaged in public diplomacy, such as tweeting about the Holocaust, and has spent significant time negotiating with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry.

A Connecticut teen in remission from Hodgkin lymphoma will remain in state custody after a judge denied her motion to return home. The state, which has overseen her forced chemotherapy treatment, views her as a flight risk and will allow her to go home only after her treatment concludes.

New research suggests Shakespeare co-wrote the play "Double Falsehood," with computer analysis showing a "landslide" match to his style. The study, published in Psychological Science, attributes the play's first half to Shakespeare and the second to a collaboration with John Fletcher.

French officials deny reports of a cell phone video from the Germanwings crash, calling them "completely wrong." Meanwhile, Lufthansa confirmed co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had a history of depression before crashing the plane, killing all 150 on board.

American Samoan veteran Emy Afalava, born on U.S. soil, is denied citizenship and voting rights, a legal anomaly rooted in a century-old Supreme Court precedent. He and other American Samoans are now suing in federal court to overturn this exception to the 14th Amendment.

Blue Bell Creameries has temporarily shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant and recalled certain products after listeria was found in a serving of ice cream. The contamination is linked to a listeria outbreak that has caused five illnesses and three deaths in Kansas.

Al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in Kenya, killing many and taking hostages. The assault highlights the group's escalating regional campaign and the deteriorating security situation in East Africa.

The U.S. has protested to Russia after a Russian SU-27 jet intercepted a U.S. reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in an "unsafe and unprofessional" manner. The Pentagon condemned the aggressive maneuvers, while Russia claimed the U.S. aircraft was flying with its transponder off. This is the latest in a series of similar incidents between the two nations' military aircraft.

A hooded angel with black wings, created by artist Phillip Hyman, has become an icon for the Black Lives Matter movement following the police killing of Walter Scott in North Charleston. The artwork, crafted from reclaimed wood and black paint, is now carried by protesters to rallies mourning Scott and symbolizing the indignity of his death.

Officer Michael Slager was fired and charged with murder after a bystander's video contradicted his account of shooting an unarmed man, Walter Scott. The footage shows Slager firing eight times as Scott fled, while initial police reports claimed Scott had taken the officer's Taser.

ISIS claimed control of part of Iraq's largest oil refinery, posting images of an assault, while Iraqi officials denied the claim and insisted they remain in full control. The strategic facility, a key target for militants, is located near Tikrit, recently retaken from ISIS.

Nashville's DA banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, a practice used four times in five years. The author argues the practice is constitutional and the public outrage is rooted in gender bias, as sterilization for male offenders is widely accepted.
Over 25,000 people have contracted Ebola in the last year, with over 10,000 fatalities. While new infections are at a low, the virus persists with unknown transmission chains still posing a risk.

The NCAA, which publicly touts its commitment to student-athletes' education, is now arguing in court it has no legal duty to ensure that education is actually delivered. The organization's stance, in response to a lawsuit over an academic fraud scandal, contradicts its long-held principles and has drawn criticism from former officials and whistleblowers.
Six people were injured in a blast and fire at a controversial chemical plant in China's Fujian province. The fire is now under control after more than 600 firefighters responded.

A bystander's video captured an officer shooting a fleeing man in the back, leading to his arrest. The author argues that police body cameras could have prevented the tragedy and restored public trust by deterring misconduct.

Venezuela's President Maduro has accused the U.S. of plotting a coup, prompting reciprocal sanctions and creating a "triangle of tension" at the Americas Summit. The diplomatic rift has complicated the anticipated U.S.-Cuba handshake, with Cuba's foreign minister publicly siding with Venezuela against the United States.

A nuclear submarine under repair at a Russian shipyard caught fire during welding work. The fire, which broke out in the submarine's insulation, poses no threat as the nuclear fuel has been unloaded and no one was injured.

Tropical storm Maysak, packing winds of 70 mph, is approaching the Philippines, prompting warnings of flash floods and landslides. Authorities have preemptively barred outdoor activities and evacuated residents ahead of its expected landfall Sunday.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly called out his son, Deion Jr., on Twitter for his "hood doughnut" obsession, reminding him of his trust fund and affluent lifestyle. The younger Sanders retweeted the comments, taking the public scolding in stride.

Guatemalan women face epidemic levels of gender-based violence, with two killed daily in a climate of impunity and deep-seated machismo culture. Despite new laws and community programs, a weak judicial system and entrenched discrimination hinder justice for victims.

Malegaon police are requiring residents to register their cattle with photos and unique features to enforce a beef ban. The move aims to create a database to investigate cow slaughter cases, following a recent incident and stricter state laws.

Lucknow police deploy pepper-spraying drones to disperse unruly crowds, a move that has drawn criticism for its authoritarian approach. The drones, which have been tested successfully, will be used during violent protests and mob attacks.

Don McLean's handwritten lyrics for his 1971 anthem "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's. The 16-page manuscript, a cultural touchstone for generations, was purchased by an unnamed buyer.

A sophisticated gang executed a daring, old-fashioned burglary at a London vault, reminiscent of classic heists. The meticulously planned raid, which targeted safety deposit boxes, is being investigated for possible inside information. Police are conducting a forensic and intelligence-led pursuit of the perpetrators.

7-Eleven is hosting a Bring-Your-Own-Cup Slurpee Day at U.S. stores Saturday, allowing customers to fill their own vessels for $1.49. The promotion, which has size and sanitation rules, is a separate event from the annual Free Slurpee Day.

Former Kentucky state senator, the first woman and person of color to serve, criticizes Rand Paul's presidential launch, calling his message of inclusion hypocritical given his record on civil rights. The author dismisses Paul's outreach as insincere, citing his opposition to landmark legislation and his stated desire to roll back progress.
A Lamborghini crashed at Walt Disney World's Exotic Driving Experience, killing a passenger. The driver lost control, causing the fatal crash.

Former NFL star Aaron Hernandez's defense rested its case in less than a day after prosecutors presented 131 witnesses over months. The case, which hinges on circumstantial evidence, is now set for jury deliberation following closing arguments.

Chinese authorities have formally detained five women's rights activists, including Wu Rongrong, for "creating disturbances" after they were arrested for planning an International Women's Day protest. The detentions, which come as China prepares to mark a major women's rights conference, are part of a broader government effort to suppress independent activism.

Martin O'Malley dismissed Hillary Clinton's "inevitable" frontrunner status, citing history and Clinton's 2008 loss. The former governor, who is teasing a presidential run, argued that a robust primary debate is needed for the Democratic Party.

Aaron Hernandez was sentenced to life in prison for the first-degree murder of Odin Lloyd. Lloyd's mother delivered a victim impact statement, describing her son as the family's backbone and expressing her grief and forgiveness.

Ted Cruz is actively courting Iowa's evangelical voters, a key bloc he hopes will propel his presidential campaign. He is leveraging his strong conservative record and personal faith to build a coalition with tea party and libertarian factions.
Marvel revealed Paul Bettany as the Vision in a new "Avengers: Age of Ultron" poster. The studio also debuted the real Daredevil suit and announced Ben Hardy as Angel for "X-Men: Apocalypse."

Nearly 1,000 migrants were rescued off Libya as the number of deaths attempting the Mediterranean crossing this year has surged to at least 480. The perilous journey, often on overcrowded vessels, continues to draw thousands from Africa and the Middle East seeking asylum in Europe.
TV5Monde regained control of one channel Thursday after a cyberattack disabled its broadcasts and social media. An Islamist group claimed responsibility, though no official claim has been made.

David Lynch has confirmed he will not direct the upcoming third season of "Twin Peaks," citing budget disputes with the network. Showtime expressed sadness over the decision but stated it hopes to proceed with the revival.
High-profile trials for Aaron Hernandez and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev conclude in Massachusetts. Sen. Rand Paul officially announced his presidential bid, while Chicago voters head to a mayoral runoff.

Tornadoes touched down in Kansas and Missouri Wednesday night, with spotters reporting twisters near Wichita and damage in Potosi. The storms, which included large hail, are expected to continue Thursday across the Midwest.
Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2008 murder of Travis Alexander. The judge imposed the sentence after two juries deadlocked on whether to impose the death penalty.

A Delaware family fell ill and was hospitalized after being exposed to a restricted pesticide, methyl bromide, in a U.S. Virgin Islands villa. The EPA is investigating the incident, which has prompted a criminal probe by the Department Justice into Terminix, the pest control company.

An outside review found Rolling Stone's reporting and editing process failed, leading to a flawed article about a UVA gang rape. The fraternity named in the story plans to pursue legal action, but faces significant legal hurdles in a potential defamation suit.

FBI agents shot and wounded a robbery suspect after a high-speed chase in Georgia, which also resulted in two agents being injured in a crash. The suspect, wanted for 32 commercial robberies, was captured following the confrontation.

Alaska Airlines Flight 448 returned to Seattle after a ramp agent was found asleep in the cargo hold, following reports of banging from passengers. The man, who fell asleep after his shift, was unharmed but the airline is investigating the security breach.

A North Carolina judge ruled that Craig Hicks, charged with the murder of three Muslim students, is eligible for the death penalty. The ruling comes as the case, stemming from a neighbor dispute, remains under investigation as a possible hate crime.

Amnesty International reports a surge in attacks on Afghan women's rights activists, urging authorities to address the persecution by the Taliban, warlords, and government officials. Despite the dangers, activists remain resilient, as demonstrated by a historic protest following the murder of Farkhunda, where women defied tradition to carry her coffin.

A New York judge has authorized serving divorce papers on a husband via Facebook private messaging. This method is seen as a modern alternative to traditional, often unreliable, forms of legal service like mail or publication. The ruling reflects the growing prevalence of online communication in legal proceedings.

Rev. Robert H. Schuller, the California televangelist and founder of the "Hour of Power" ministry and Crystal Cathedral, has died at 88. He pioneered televangelism with a message of "possibility thinking," but his ministry later collapsed amid family and financial disputes.
Four workers died and 45 were injured in a massive fire on a Mexican oil rig off the coast. The blaze, which raged for hours, was extinguished by Wednesday night with no reported oil spill.

Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback signed a first-in-the-nation law banning a common second-trimester abortion procedure. The law, which opponents call one of the most restrictive in the U.S., is expected to face legal challenges.
CCTV host Bi Fujian sparked controversy after a video showed him cursing Mao Zedong during

Kentucky guard Andrew Harrison apologized after a hot mic caught him using a racial slur toward Wisconsin's Frank Kaminsky following their loss. Kaminsky accepted the apology, stating he was "over it" and that the matter was resolved.
"Arrested Development" will return for a fifth season of 17 episodes, executive producer Brian Grazer announced. Netflix has not yet verified the news, and it is unknown if the full cast will return.

The Large Hadron Collider has restarted after a two-year shutdown, with scientists circulating the first beams. The world's largest particle accelerator will now smash protons at near light-speed to recreate Big Bang conditions and probe fundamental physics questions.

An Iranian military aircraft flew within 50 yards of a U.S. Navy helicopter in the Persian Gulf, an incident U.S. officials believe may have been ordered by a local commander. The unsafe maneuver, which occurred amid nuclear negotiations, has prompted the U.S. to consider a formal protest against Iran.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts in the Boston Marathon bombing trial, making him eligible for the death penalty. The case now moves to a penalty phase where a jury will decide whether he should be executed.
Indian police arrested four FabIndia employees after a minister found a security camera in a store's changing room. The staff face voyeurism charges; the store manager remains at large.

Iran plans to lift its decades-long ban on women attending some men's sports events, starting with indoor games, a top sports official said. The move comes amid international pressure, with FIFA previously calling the ban "intolerable."

Indian software pioneer Ramalinga Raju and nine others were sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in a $1.6 billion corporate fraud. The former Satyam Computers chairman was also fined $804,000 for the massive accounting scandal.

Elizabeth Sedway was removed from an Alaska Airlines flight in Hawaii after an employee noted her illness and called a doctor, despite her claims of having cancer. The airline apologized, refunded her tickets, and paid for her overnight stay after she missed her chemotherapy appointment and a connecting flight.
Turkish singer Kayahan, famed for his love songs, died of cancer in Istanbul at age 66. The prolific songwriter, who rose to fame after his 1991 album, was mourned by Prime Minister Davutoglu.

Israeli PM Netanyahu criticized the Iran nuclear deal, calling it "bad" and advocating for a third alternative of increased pressure. His remarks fueled U.S. political sparring, with Democrats defending the framework and Republicans contending a successor could negotiate a better agreement.

Shootings at a U.S. Census Bureau headquarters and a Washington restaurant, stemming from a domestic kidnapping, left a guard and an officer wounded. The suspect was also injured after a police chase and shootout.

Imprisoned soldier Chelsea Manning has joined Twitter, dictating tweets to a firm that will post them on her behalf. The former Army intelligence analyst, serving a 35-year sentence for leaking classified documents, is not allowed internet access.

Hip-hop star Nelly was arrested in Tennessee on drug charges after a trooper stopped his bus and found methamphetamine, marijuana, and drug paraphernalia. The 40-year-old rapper, whose real name is Cornell Haynes, was charged with felony drug possession and later released on bond.

A Delaware father is improving while his two sons remain in critical condition after possibly being exposed to a restricted pesticide at a U.S. Virgin Islands resort. The EPA has confirmed the presence of methyl bromide in the villa, and the Department of Justice has launched a criminal investigation.

Online media has become a primary alternative to state-controlled press in authoritarian nations, attracting dissidents despite severe risks. Governments across Asia increasingly use legal persecution and imprisonment to silence online critics, while in weaker states, bloggers face violent attacks with near-total impunity.

"The Vampire Diaries" star Nina Dobrev announced she is leaving the show after its sixth season, disappointing fans who felt her departure would ruin the series. Fans reacted angrily, criticizing producers for continuing the show without her, while producers stated they supported her decision to move on.

ISIS stormed the Yarmouk camp near Damascus, prompting a government siege and bombardment that has trapped civilians amid widespread destruction. The once-vibrant Palestinian neighborhood is now a besieged war zone, with residents facing starvation and relentless violence as international aid fails to reach them.

NASA scientists detailed plans to search for extraterrestrial life over the next two decades, noting the discovery of thousands of exoplanets, including billions potentially habitable. While primitive life is considered likely, the odds of finding intelligent, communicative life are deemed extremely slim due to vast time and distance scales.
A Massachusetts man faces murder charges after human remains were found in a duffel bag and a nearby common area. The victim was identified as a 26-year-old man who knew the suspect.
Kanye West settled a civil lawsuit with paparazzo Daniel Ramos, whom he assaulted at LAX in 2013. The settlement included an apology from West to Ramos, who had sought damages for the attack.

Obama's political legacy is tied to the Iran nuclear deal, which critics argue has weakened U.S. standing and strengthened Iran. The agreement allows Iran to retain significant nuclear capabilities while sanctions are lifted, fueling regional instability and a nuclear arms race.

A bystander's video led to the arrest of a police officer for murder after he shot an unarmed man, exposing conflicting police reports. The incident highlights a critical lack of federal data on police use of force, as a 1994 law mandating such data collection has gone unenforced for decades.

Five Americans exposed to Ebola in West Africa have been released from a Nebraska hospital after a three-week monitoring period. None of the clinicians developed the virus, though one was treated for a heart-related issue.

Mark Ronson's "Uptown Funk!" featuring Bruno Mars logs a 13th week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming the longest-leading single of the 2010s. The track also joins an elite group of just 10 songs in chart history to spend at least 13 weeks at the summit.

April 8 was "Rex Manning Day," a pop culture holiday from the film "Empire Records." Other famous film dates include April 14 from "Titanic," October 3 from "Mean Girls," and October 21, 2015, from "Back to the Future Part II."

Critically-panned film "Grace of Monaco," starring Nicole Kidman, will premiere on Lifetime after The Weinstein Co. sells U.S. distribution rights. The studio bypassed a theatrical release following the film's poor international performance and director Harvey Weinstein's dispute over its final cut.

Tokyo's Shibuya ward passed an ordinance to issue "partnership certificates" to same-sex couples, granting them limited rights like hospital visitation and co-signing leases. The move, hailed as a significant step by activists, is not legally binding but aims to increase visibility for Japan's LGBT community.

California's historic drought is driving up food prices nationwide due to its role as a major agricultural producer. The crisis has also mandated water cuts and altered tourism, though wine quality has unexpectedly improved.

University of Michigan will screen "American Sniper" after reversing a cancellation decision that sparked backlash. The university stated the initial move was inconsistent with its commitment to free expression.

Amy Schumer's opening monologue and Channing Tatum's twerk for Jennifer Lopez were highlights at the 2015 MTV Movie Awards. The show also featured an awkward archery fail and a misfire by Shailene Woodley during her acceptance speech.

A 20-30 foot fiberglass boat fragment suspected to be from Japan's 2011 tsunami was towed ashore in Oregon. The debris, carrying live Japanese fish, poses a low ecological threat and will be disposed of, while the fish will be taken to a local aquarium.

Nigerian President-elect Buhari marked the anniversary of the Chibok schoolgirls' kidnapping, vowing to combat Boko Haram. Over 200 girls remain missing one year after their abduction, as the militant group continues to terrorize the region.

Easter's Holy Triduum—Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday—marks a spiritual progression from suffering to resurrection. This pattern, reflecting the human condition, offers a timeless hope that resists secular commercialization.

Kenya froze 86 accounts linked to suspected Al-Shabaab supporters following the Garissa university attack that killed 147 people. The government also launched airstrikes on militant camps in Somalia and offered a reward for the attack's alleged organizer.

Jia Jiang launched a "100 Days of Rejection" project to overcome his fear of being turned down after his startup failed. The project, which involved making unusual requests of strangers, went viral and led to a book deal and public speaking career. Jiang now aims to help others see rejection as an opportunity rather than an obstacle.

Attorney General Eric Holder has reaffirmed a strict prohibition on federal agents soliciting prostitutes, citing links to human trafficking. The directive follows reports of misconduct by DEA agents and comes with the threat of suspension or firing for violations.

Authorities in North Carolina are investigating the killing of a Wayne Community College employee as a possible hate crime. The suspect, who was arrested in Florida, had a motive related to the victim's sexuality and is being investigated for potential gang ties.

China staged a public mass sentencing in Xinjiang, part of its "Strike Hard" anti-terrorism campaign. Globally, executions rose in 2014 as governments used the death penalty as a flawed deterrent to crime and terrorism, though overall numbers fell slightly.

A Duke student admitted to hanging a noose from a tree on campus and has left the school to face a conduct review. The incident prompted a campus protest and ongoing criminal investigations into whether others were involved.

Emmy-winning actor Richard Dysart, famed for his role as Leland McKenzie on "L.A. Law," has died at 86 after a long illness. He was a prolific character actor who also appeared in numerous films and television productions.

Easter's date is determined by the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox, a method that can cause it to differ from the Orthodox celebration. The holiday's secular traditions, such as the Easter Bunny and colored eggs, have pagan origins and were popularized by German immigrants.

Comedian Chris Rock is documenting his recent traffic stops on Twitter, highlighting the issue of racial profiling. His posts, which include photos of police encounters, have sparked a debate about "driving while black" and how African Americans should respond to it.
Lynyrd Skynyrd original drummer Bob Burns, 64, died in a single-car crash in Georgia Friday night. Burns was a founding member of the Southern rock band before leaving in 1975.

A photo of a cat on stairs has sparked viral debate online, with users divided over whether the animal is going up or down. The image, first posted on Imgur, has ignited a new social media optical illusion trend.

US and partners reach a framework deal in Lausanne to effectively block Iran from building a nuclear weapon. The agreement faces significant political pushback from US and Israeli opponents despite its rigorous inspection regime and verifiable limits on Iran's program.

UVA remains under investigation for its handling of sexual assault, having never expelled a student for the offense, despite a retracted Rolling Stone article sparking a national conversation. The retraction has raised fears that progress on the issue will be set back, as survivors may now be hesitant to come forward.

Indiana Pacers forward Chris Copeland was stabbed outside a New York City nightclub early Wednesday. Two Atlanta Hawks players were arrested on obstruction charges after the incident, while a suspect in the stabbing was also taken into custody.
Twisted Sister will embark on a final tour, "Forty and F*ck It," to mark its 40th anniversary. The band will honor late drummer A.J. Pero with two special shows and feature Mike Portnoy on drums.

Scientologist John Travolta dismissed the critical HBO documentary on his faith, calling it negative and based on disgruntled hearsay. The actor, a prominent member of the church, praised Scientology as a positive experience that helped him through personal tragedy.

"Furious 7" earned a record $146 million in its opening weekend. The film's emotional ending, a tribute to the late Paul Walker, resonated deeply with audiences and sparked widespread praise on social media.

"Game of Thrones" season five premieres globally, with story arcs converging and surpassing the books. Expect bigger battles, a focus on Stark daughters and Cersei, and a look at the common people's breaking point.

Several individuals survived being stranded at sea for weeks or months through extreme resourcefulness and luck. Survivors included a man adrift for 13 months, a fisherman rescued after 12 days, and a man who survived a tsunami by clinging to debris.

"Star Wars" films become available for digital download, featuring rare behind-the-scenes footage. The collection includes a first look at the saga's first gay character and details on creating alien sound effects.

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all 30 counts for the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing and its aftermath. Survivors expressed relief that he was being held accountable, though many stated the verdict could not bring true justice or erase their pain.

A Philadelphia mother faces multiple charges after allegedly abandoning her 21-year-old quadriplegic son in a park for four days. The man was found suffering from exposure and dehydration before being hospitalized. The mother was arrested in Maryland and will be extradited to face the charges.

Walmart's opposition to an Arkansas religious freedom law forced the governor to veto the bill, signaling a shift in corporate and Republican support for gay rights. The retailer's stance, backed by other major businesses, highlights a growing corporate push for nondiscrimination policies that impact the political landscape.

A lapsed Catholic credits Pope Francis with reawakening her faith, citing his humble, non-judgmental tone and actions. The Pope's approach, described as returning to the Gospel's foundation of love and openness, contrasts with the author's past experience of feeling rejected by the Church.

Mary Kay Letourneau Fualaau and her former student husband, Vili Fualaau, are still together and will mark their 10th anniversary. The couple, whose relationship began when he was 13 and she was his teacher, will discuss their marriage in an upcoming ABC interview.

Hillary Clinton's 2016 candidacy makes her the barometer for gender equality in the U.S., a burden no male candidate faces. Her win or loss risks being misinterpreted as a referendum on women's political viability, overshadowing systemic issues.

Amnesty International alleges governments are using terrorism fears to justify executions, citing Pakistan and China. While global executions fell 22%, death sentences spiked 28%, with China and the US among the top users.

Japan's defense minister confirmed to parliament that the Air Self Defense Force has never encountered an extraterrestrial UFO. The statement came in response to a question from flamboyant lawmaker Antonio Inoki, who also claimed to have seen a UFO.

Mark Wahlberg will star in and produce "Patriots' Day," a film about the Boston Marathon bombing from the perspective of Police Commissioner Ed Davis. The project, from CBS Films, will use research and footage from CBS News' "60 Minutes."

Martin O'Malley and Jim Webb, potential Democratic presidential candidates, displayed contrasting styles at an Iowa event. O'Malley actively engaged in retail politics, while Webb remained more reserved. Both face steep odds against the likely front-runner, Hillary Clinton.

Nine British citizens, including four children, were arrested in Turkey for allegedly attempting to illegally cross into Syria. The group, consisting of three men, two women, and four children, was apprehended at the Turkey-Syria border. The UK Foreign Office is aware of the arrests and is seeking information from Turkish authorities.

FedEx faces a 15-count indictment for allegedly transporting illegal prescription drugs and money laundering. The company argues it is protected by the "common carrier" exception, as it had no knowledge of the shipments. The DOJ contends FedEx knowingly facilitated the illegal drug trade.

Kenyans mourn 147 victims of a Garissa University attack, using social media to share their stories after authorities failed to release a list. The attack, Kenya's deadliest since 1998, saw Al-Shabaab separate and kill Christians, while one attacker was identified as the son of a government official.

Swedish photographer Johan Bavman documents fathers using the country's 480-day paid parental leave to promote gender equality. Despite the policy, only 12% of couples share leave equally, with most women still taking the majority of time off.

Obama affirmed his commitment to Israel's military edge and defense, defending the Iran nuclear deal as a critical opportunity to curb Tehran's nuclear ambitions despite Israeli and Republican criticism. The deal, which would reduce Iran's centrifuges and increase inspections, is being negotiated for a final agreement by June 30.

Indiana's new Religious Freedom Restoration Act has ignited a national debate over religious liberty and potential discrimination. Similar state laws have led to rare but significant legal victories for religious minorities, including cases involving Native American eagle feathers and a sacramental tea.

Five Chinese feminists face up to five years in prison on charges of disturbing public order for their gender equality campaign. The activists' detention has drawn international criticism, with prosecutors set to decide on formal charges.

Selena's family is creating a digital, hologram-like version of the late Tejano star for new music, videos, and a potential 2018 tour. The project, "Selena the One," aims to expand her legacy using new technology and is seeking fan funding via an Indiegogo campaign.

Former Rep. Michele Bachmann compared President Obama's Iran deal to the Germanwings co-pilot who crashed his plane, drawing widespread criticism. The Minnesota Republican has a history of making controversial remarks about the president's Iran policy.

Ryan Gosling's directorial debut, "Lost River," is a divisive film centered on the decaying yet resilient city of Detroit. The project began as a documentary effort to capture the city's crumbling housing projects before their demolition. The film explores themes of urban decay and rebirth, aiming to show Detroit's struggle beyond its dereliction.

A 19-year-old UK national was charged with terror offenses upon his return to Britain from Turkey. Yahya Rashid was arrested at Luton airport and charged with preparing for and assisting acts of terrorism.

Performing the national anthem can make or break a celebrity's reputation. Vince Neil's recent rendition joins a long list of infamous versions by stars like Roseanne Barr and Michael Bolton, while Whitney Houston's performance remains a gold standard.

WWI graffiti from nearly 2,000 soldiers has been discovered in a vast underground French quarry. Photographer Jeff Gusky, who found the inscriptions, calls the site a "treasure trove" that offers a poignant human connection to the past.

Palestinian Authority became the 123rd member of the International Criminal Court, granting the body jurisdiction over alleged crimes in Palestinian territories. The move, opposed by Israel and the U.S., allows the ICC to pursue possible war crimes investigations against Israelis and Palestinians.

Anthony Ray Hinton was released from Alabama's death row after 30 years when the state dismissed charges against him. A judge granted the motion after new evidence cast doubt on the conviction, which Hinton had always maintained was unjust.

Tax Day has become a happy spending spree for most Americans, who receive an average $3,000 refund, aided by free filing services. This positive ending overshadows the system's deep flaws, including complexity and bias against wage earners in favor of the wealthy.

Jordan Spieth maintained a commanding lead after the third round at the Masters, despite a late double bogey. Rory McIlroy, Tiger Woods, and Phil Mickelson all made moves but could not close the gap on the 21-year-old leader.

Liana Barrientos, 39, pleaded not guilty to charges of fraud for lying on a marriage license application as part of an immigration scam. She has been married 10 times, sometimes to eight men at once, to help them gain permanent residency.

Memories Pizza in Indiana became a flashpoint after its owners stated they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding, citing religious beliefs. The statement ignited a firestorm of boycotts and online harassment, but also prompted a massive crowdfunding campaign that raised over $842,000 for the business.

Mindy Kaling's brother, Vijay Chokalingam, admitted to fraudulently posing as African-American to gain medical school admission, a scheme he now details in a book. Despite his claims of receiving preferential treatment, he was rejected by top schools and faced racial profiling, while his sister's career was aided by a diversity initiative.
Antarctica recorded a temperature of 63.5°F (15.5°C) on March 24, a potential record high. A UN committee of experts has been formed to verify the measurement's validity.

U.S. officials have abandoned the spring timeframe for an Iraqi-led offensive to retake Mosul from ISIS, citing the operation's complexity. While ISIS has been degraded and the campaign has begun with airstrikes, officials stress patience, noting the operation will require more time and capacity.

Irish betting firm Paddy Power deleted a controversial tweet that linked Liverpool's "Kop beatings" to police shootings of African-American men. The company apologized, calling it a joke, but faced widespread condemnation on social media.
Mother of quadriplegic son faces attempted murder charge after abandoning him in Philadelphia park. She is in Maryland custody pending treatment before extradition.

South Korean court indicted Kim Ki-Jong on charges of attempted murder and assaulting a U.S. envoy for stabbing Ambassador Mark Lippert. The attack, which left Lippert with severe facial wounds, was allegedly motivated by opposition to joint U.S.-South Korea military drills.
"19 Kids and Counting" star Jill Dillard has given birth to her first child, a son named Israel David. The baby, born a week late, is the first grandchild for the Duggar family.

Universal's "Furious 7" is projected to open with a massive $135 million-$138 million in North America, the biggest debut since late 2013. The film, the last to feature the late Paul Walker, is also on track for a record-breaking worldwide debut approaching $300 million.

Secret Service supervisor Xavier Morales is on leave after a female employee accused him of sexual assault and grabbing her arms during a March 31 incident. The scandal is the latest in a series of high-profile missteps for the agency, which is already under scrutiny for security lapses and leadership failures.

Hillary Clinton announced her 2016 presidential candidacy, touting her experience and strength as a top-tier candidate. However, she faces significant challenges, including questions of authenticity, energizing the Democratic base, and navigating potential liabilities from her husband and past controversies.

The DOJ will begin negotiations to restructure the Ferguson Police Department, which it found engaged in a pattern of racial discrimination. The move follows protests over the Michael Brown shooting and the election of two new black city council members.
Etihad Airways lost a cat after its carrier was damaged upon arrival at JFK Airport. The airline is investigating the incident and searching for the missing pet.

Louis Jordan, 37, was rescued after drifting for 66 days in the Atlantic Ocean following a storm that capsized his sailboat. The man survived by collecting rainwater and catching fish with a hand net before being spotted by a container ship.
